feedback.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y=4{e}^{-x}.
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +2 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda +1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-2$ or $\lambda =-1$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-2x}+B{e}^{-x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $4{e}^{-x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $-1$, which coincides with one of the roots of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha x{e}^{-x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha (1-x){e}^{-x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (x-2){e}^{-x}.
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (x-2){e}^{-x}+3(\alpha (1-x){e}^{-x})+2(\alpha x{e}^{-x}) & =4{e}^{-x} \\ (x-2+3-3x+2x)\alpha {e}^{-x} & =4{e}^{-x} \\ \alpha {e}^{-x} & =4{e}^{-x} \\ \alpha  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=4x{e}^{-x}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-2x}+B{e}^{-x}+4x{e}^{-x}.
$$
